title: Which two digits do you swap to get the biggest number?
description: Joseph swaps two digits of his bus ticket number. The video finds the swap that gives the largest number and the swap that gives the smallest.
teaching_notes: One idea: the leftmost place is worth the most, so put the biggest digit there for the largest number. Watch for children who swap the two biggest digits.

source: Swap two digits of 2,935 to make the largest number and the
video_script.why: The child knows place values but has not yet used them to choose which two digits to swap.
video_script.substitution: Move the biggest digit into the leftmost place for the largest number, and keep or put the smallest digit there for the smallest.
video_script.anchor: Joseph's bus ticket number whose digits he may swap
video_script.wrong_move: Chintu swaps the two biggest digits, nine and five, and gets 2,539. The nine lands in the ones place and the thousands place still holds the small digit two.
video_script.payoff_line: the largest number is nine thousand, two hundred and thirty-five

final_answer.spoken: largest nine thousand two hundred and thirty-five by swapping two and nine, smallest two thousand three hundred and ninety-five by swapping nine and three

maths_rules: ticket 2,935: thousands 2, hundreds 9, tens 3, ones 5; the leftmost place is worth the most
slip: swap 9 and 5 gives 2,539, which is not the largest
largest: put 9, the biggest digit, in the thousands place; swap 2 and 9 to get 9,235
smallest: 2 is already the smallest digit and is in the thousands place; keep it; put 3, the next smallest, in the hundreds place; swap 9 and 3 to get 2,395
your turn: 6,184; largest swaps 6 and 8 to give 8,164; smallest swaps 6 and 1 to give 1,684; never shown
video_script.design: One idea: the leftmost place is worth the most, so it decides. Wrong idea: swap the two biggest digits. The ticket with four digit boxes stays on the stage.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a bus ticket marked 2,935 with its four digits in boxes; two curved arrows over two boxes; two empty boxes labelled largest and smallest

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='ticket'/>Joseph has a bus ticket numbered two thousand, nine hundred and thirty-five.
<bookmark mark='rule'/>He may swap the places of only two digits in the number.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Which swap makes the largest number, and which swap makes the smallest number?

beats.on_screen: the anchor holds still and gets an accent underline

marks.stop: the anchor is underlined in the accent colour

narration: <bookmark mark='stop'/>Stop the video. Say your answer out loud.

beats.on_screen: the ticket digits 2, 9, 3, 5 sit in boxes labelled thousands, hundreds, tens and ones; an arrow along the boxes shows worth growing towards the left

marks.pv: the boxes for thousands and hundreds are labelled
marks.tens: the boxes for tens and ones are labelled
marks.left: an arrow along the boxes shows worth growing to the left
marks.why: a digit slides one box left and its value grows

narration: <bookmark mark='pv'/>The two is in the thousands place. The nine is in the hundreds place.
<bookmark mark='tens'/>The three is in the tens place, and the five is in the ones place.
<bookmark mark='left'/>The place on the left is worth the most.
<bookmark mark='why'/>A digit moved one place left becomes ten times as big.

beats.on_screen: Chintu's bubble shows swap 9 and 5; the nine slides to the ones box and its worth shrinks; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.chintu: Chintu's bubble appears with swap 9 and 5
marks.move: the nine slides to the ones box and shrinks in worth
marks.strike: the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

narration: [chintu] <bookmark mark='chintu'/>Nine and five are the biggest digits, so I swap nine and five for the largest.
<bookmark mark='move'/>That moves the nine into the ones place, where it is worth only nine.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>It also leaves the thousands place with a small digit.

beats.on_screen: the 2 and the 9 swap places; the ticket reads 9,235; the answer card shows largest 9,235

marks.big: the 9 box glows and an arrow points to the thousands box
marks.pay: the ticket now reads 9,235 and the answer card shows largest 9,235

narration: <bookmark mark='big'/>For the largest number, put the biggest digit, nine, in the thousands place.
<bookmark mark='swap'/>Swap the two and the nine.
<bookmark mark='pay'/>The largest number is nine thousand, two hundred and thirty-five.

beats.on_screen: the 2 is locked; the 9 and the 3 swap places; the ticket reads 2,395; the answer card shows smallest 2,395

marks.two: the 2 box is locked with a small padlock
marks.next: the 3 box glows and an arrow points to the hundreds box
marks.ans: the ticket reads 2,395 and the answer card shows smallest 2,395

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Two is already the smallest digit, and it sits in the thousands place, so keep it there.
<bookmark mark='next'/>Put the next smallest digit, three, in the hundreds place.
<bookmark mark='swap'/>Swap the nine and the three.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The smallest number is two thousand, three hundred and ninety-five.

beats.on_screen: the stage clears except the ticket; two lines appear: biggest digit to the leftmost place for the largest; smallest digit to the leftmost place for the smallest; then a new ticket marked 6,184 with two empty boxes

marks.one: the line biggest digit to the leftmost place appears
marks.two: the line smallest digit to the leftmost place appears
marks.turn: a new ticket marked 6,184 appears with two empty boxes

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>For a large number, put the biggest digit in the leftmost place.
<bookmark mark='two'/>For a small number, put the smallest digit there, if it is not already there.
<bookmark mark='turn'/>Your turn. Swap two digits of six thousand, one hundred and eighty-four to make the largest and the smallest number.
